terms.why: In-the-money options have intrinsic value; out-of-the-money options are made up only of time value, which falls to zero at expiry.
terms.how: Time value shrinks faster as expiry nears.
terms.formula: Call intrinsic value = max(Price − Strike, 0); Put intrinsic value = max(Strike − Price, 0)
terms.finlit: On FinLit's option chain, in-the-money calls and puts are shaded.

terms.meaning: A number that tracks the combined price of a chosen basket of stocks, such as the 50 largest companies on the NSE.
terms.why: It shows in one figure whether 'the market' or a sector rose or fell.
terms.how: Compare your portfolio's return with a suitable index to see if your choices beat simply owning the market.

terms.meaning: A mutual fund or ETF that simply copies an index such as the Nifty 50, at low cost.
terms.why: Most active funds fail to beat their index over long periods after fees.
terms.how: A low-cost index fund is a sensible core holding for many investors.

terms.meaning: The price-to-earnings ratio of a whole index, such as the Nifty 50, from the combined market value and earnings of its companies. An index's P/B and dividend yield work the same way.
terms.why: It shows whether the market as a whole is priced high or low against its own history.
terms.how: Compare it with the index's own long-run range. A high P/E can last for years, and changes in the index's members also move it.
terms.formula: Index P/E = Combined market value of members ÷ Combined earnings of members
terms.finlit: FinLit's index valuation history marks an upper and a lower usual level around the index's own past readings.

terms.meaning: The NSE's 'fear gauge': the volatility the options market expects in the Nifty over the next 30 days, as a yearly percentage.
terms.why: It rises when investors are nervous.
terms.how: Below about 15 is calm, above about 25 is fearful.

terms.meaning: The rate at which prices in general rise, reducing what money can buy. In India it is usually tracked by the consumer price index (CPI).
terms.why: Returns only matter after inflation: 7% return with 6% inflation is about 1% real gain.
terms.how: Aim for long-run returns comfortably above inflation.
terms.formula: Inflation % = (CPI now − CPI a year ago) ÷ CPI a year ago × 100

terms.meaning: Insolvency is when a company cannot pay its debts. India's Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC) sets a process to revive or sell such companies.
terms.why: Shareholders usually lose most or all of their money in insolvency.
terms.how: A company in an insolvency process carries extra risk; read the resolution plan before treating it as a turnaround.

terms.meaning: A bank's interest expense as a share of its total income; a FinLit screener filter for lenders.
terms.why: Lower means cheaper funding relative to what the bank earns.
terms.how: Use it with NIM and CASA to compare lenders' funding strength.

terms.meaning: Operating profit (EBIT) divided by interest expense: how many times over the company can pay its interest.
terms.why: Low coverage means a small fall in profit could make interest hard to pay.
terms.how: Below 1.5 is weak, above 3 is generally comfortable; FinLit flags 'weak interest cover' as a red flag.
terms.formula: Interest coverage = EBIT ÷ Interest expense

terms.meaning: An interim dividend is declared during the financial year; a final dividend is proposed after the year ends and approved at the annual general meeting.
terms.why: Many companies pay both, so the year's total is their sum.
terms.how: Check FinLit's dividend history for the months a company usually pays.

terms.meaning: The yearly return at which the present value of an investment's cash flows equals zero.
terms.why: It lets you compare projects or investments with different cash-flow patterns.
terms.how: XIRR is the same idea for irregular dates.
terms.formula: 0 = Sum of CF_t ÷ (1 + IRR)^t

terms.meaning: An intraday trade is bought and sold on the same day; a delivery trade means the shares move into your demat account and you hold them.
terms.why: Intraday trading carries different charges and much higher risk.
terms.how: FinLit's research is built for delivery investors who hold for months or years.

terms.term: Intrinsic value and margin of safety
terms.meaning: Intrinsic value is an estimate of what a business is really worth based on its future cash flows. Margin of safety is the gap when the price is well below that estimate.
terms.why: Estimates can be wrong; a price below the estimate leaves room for error.
terms.how: If you estimate a share is worth ₹500, a price of ₹350 is a 30% margin of safety.

terms.meaning: How many days, on average, goods sit in stock before being sold.
terms.why: Fewer days means less cash tied up and less risk of stock going obsolete.
terms.how: Rising inventory days can be an early sign of slowing demand.
terms.formula: Inventory days = Inventory ÷ Cost of goods sold × 365

terms.meaning: Raw materials, work in progress and finished goods the company holds but has not yet sold.
terms.why: Inventory ties up cash and can lose value if it goes out of fashion or spoils.
terms.how: Rising inventory with flat sales often means demand is weakening.

terms.meaning: IPO shares are split into reserved portions for different types of investor: qualified institutional buyers (QIB), non-institutional investors (NII) and retail individual investors (RII), plus optional employee and shareholder quotas.
terms.why: Each category has its own demand and allotment rules.
terms.how: For profitable companies the usual split is up to 50% QIB, at least 15% NII and at least 35% retail. Loss-making companies must give at least 75% to QIBs and at most 10% to retail.

terms.meaning: Slides a company publishes with its results or at events, summarising performance, strategy and outlook.
terms.why: It is the quickest way to understand what the company wants investors to focus on.
terms.how: Treat it as the company's view; confirm key claims in the actual financial statements.

terms.meaning: The first time a company sells its shares to the public and lists on a stock exchange.
terms.why: It is the only time ordinary investors can buy shares directly from the company and its early owners.
terms.how: Read why the company is raising money and who is selling before applying; listing-day excitement is not a reason.

terms.meaning: International Securities Identification Number: a 12-character code that identifies one security, or one plan and option of a mutual fund, worldwide.
terms.why: Different plans and options of a fund have different ISINs and NAVs. The ISIN is the exact way to be sure you mean the same one.
terms.how: Match the ISIN, not just the fund name, when you compare data from two places.
terms.finlit: FinLit shows the ISIN AMFI gives for each scheme's growth units.

terms.meaning: The final price per share at which the IPO shares are allotted.
terms.why: Listing gains and losses are measured against it.
terms.how: Market cap at the issue price shows how the company is valued; compare that with listed peers.

terms.meaning: The total value of shares offered in the IPO, fresh issue and offer for sale together, such as ₹837 crore.
terms.why: Very large issues need broad demand; very small ones can be easy to manipulate after listing.
terms.how: Compare issue size with the company's market cap to see how much is being sold.

terms.meaning: A business set up by two or more partners who share control, costs and profits while staying separate companies.
terms.why: Joint ventures let companies enter new markets or share large investments.
terms.how: Check how a JV is accounted for; its revenue is often not included in the parent's figures.

terms.meaning: The first record of a transaction in a company's books, showing the same amount as a debit in one account and a credit in another.
terms.why: Every number in the financial statements starts as journal entries.
terms.how: You rarely need this as an investor; it explains why the books always balance.
terms.formula: Total debits = Total credits

terms.meaning: A bond with a low credit rating, paying higher interest because the risk of default is higher.
terms.why: The extra interest compensates for real risk of losing money.
terms.how: Keep only a small share of savings in low-rated debt, if any.

terms.meaning: An illegal practice of moving money between accounts to exploit clearing delays and create fake balances.
terms.why: It is fraud and is prosecuted.
terms.how: Watch for unexplained circular transactions in any company or account you review.

terms.meaning: A number that tracks how well a business is doing on what matters most, such as same-store sales for a retailer or users for a telecom firm.
terms.why: KPIs often move before financial results do.
terms.how: Find the two or three KPIs management highlights and track them each quarter.

terms.meaning: Mandatory identity and address checks before opening a bank, demat, broker or mutual fund account.
terms.why: KYC prevents fraud and money laundering.
terms.how: One KYC through a KYC registration agency usually works across brokers and fund houses.

terms.term: Large cap, mid cap and small cap
terms.meaning: Size groups based on market value. In India, the 100 largest listed companies are large caps, the next 150 mid caps, and the rest small caps; the smallest are often called micro caps.
terms.why: Smaller companies can grow faster but their prices swing more and their shares can be harder to sell.
terms.how: Check the size group before comparing returns or valuations; a small cap and a large cap are different kinds of bet.
terms.finlit: FinLit's sector pages use AMFI's list for the last half-year: the top 100 companies by average market cap are large caps, the next 150 mid caps. The company size filter uses rupee bands instead (see Company size bands).

terms.term: Last traded price (LTP) and closing price
terms.meaning: The LTP is the price of the most recent trade. The closing price is the official price at the end of the trading day, calculated by the exchange from the last half hour of trades.
terms.why: Returns, charts and most ratios use the closing price.
terms.how: During market hours (9:15 am to 3:30 pm on weekdays) prices move; after the close they stay fixed until the next session.
aliases: Last traded price and closing price

terms.meaning: The investment bank that manages the IPO: due diligence, pricing, marketing and paperwork.
terms.why: Their track record with past IPOs is worth a look.
terms.how: SEBI publishes past IPO performance by lead manager.

terms.meaning: A FinLit flag for a stock that closes at a 52-week high while its industry index is still well below its own high.
terms.why: A stock making new highs while its group is still down has held up better than its peers.
terms.how: Read it with the business scores: price and breadth flags say nothing about whether a business is sound.
terms.finlit: The flag is raised when the industry index is 10% or more below its high (15% or more is the full flag), and stays live for 60 sessions after the last such high.

terms.meaning: FinLit's plain description of how a share's last 12 months compare with its closest peers, measured against the peer group's sector index: Leader, In line or Laggard.
terms.why: Within a sector the best and worst shares are often far apart, so where a share sits in its group adds to how the sector did.
terms.how: The label describes the past. FinLit's test on weekly prices back to 2005 found only a small, sector-dependent tendency for leaders to stay ahead, and leaders fell as hard as others in 2008 and 2020.
terms.finlit: Leader means the top 30% of peers and ahead of the sector index over 12 months; Laggard the bottom 30% and behind it; everything else is In line. 'Gaining' or 'weakening' marks a 3-month relative return of +5 points or more, or −5 or less. Labels refresh weekly after Friday's close and must come out the same two weeks running.

terms.meaning: Using borrowed money to increase the size of a business or an investment. It magnifies both gains and losses.
terms.why: Leverage can make good years great and bad years dangerous.
terms.how: Check whether the company grows without needing ever more debt.
terms.formula: Leverage ratio = Total debt ÷ Total equity

terms.meaning: Money or obligations a company owes to others: loans, unpaid bills, taxes due, customer advances.
terms.why: Liabilities must be paid, whatever happens to profits.
terms.how: Compare short-term liabilities with cash and short-term assets to judge whether bills can be met.
terms.formula: Liabilities = Assets − Equity

terms.term: Liquid ETF (1-day rate or overnight ETF)
terms.meaning: An ETF that lends money for one day at a time, for example to banks through overnight lending, and so holds very short-term debt.
terms.why: Its price barely moves, so it is used to park cash, and the money earned is often paid out as a dividend.
terms.how: Because the income is often paid out, its price return can look close to zero. Check how the fund house handles the income.

terms.term: Liquid fund and money market fund
terms.meaning: Debt funds that hold very short-term instruments: liquid funds hold securities maturing in up to 91 days, and money market funds hold money-market instruments maturing in up to a year.
terms.why: They are used to park money for days or months with little movement in value.
terms.how: They are low-risk, not risk-free: check the credit quality of what they hold. Liquid funds charge a small exit load on redemptions within the first week.

terms.meaning: How quickly something can be turned into cash without losing value. For a company, its ability to meet short-term bills; for a stock, how easily it can be bought or sold.
terms.why: An illiquid stock can be hard to sell at a fair price when you need to.
terms.how: Check average daily traded value when researching small companies.

terms.meaning: The listing date is when IPO shares start trading. Listing gain or loss is the difference between the first trading price and the issue price.
terms.why: Many investors apply for listing gains, but they are not guaranteed.
terms.how: Decide beforehand whether you are investing for the long term or the listing day.

terms.meaning: The loan amount as a percentage of the value of the asset securing it, such as a house or gold.
terms.why: Lenders cap LTVs to protect against falling asset prices.
terms.how: Lower LTV means a bigger down payment and usually better loan terms.
terms.formula: LTV % = Loan amount ÷ Asset value × 100

terms.meaning: A period during which certain shareholders cannot sell. Promoters' minimum stake of 20% is generally locked for 18 months, the rest for 6 months, along with most pre-IPO investors.
terms.why: When lock-ins end, a wave of shares can be sold.
terms.how: Note lock-in expiry dates in the prospectus for stocks you hold.

terms.meaning: Only borrowings due after more than a year, divided by equity.
terms.why: Long-term debt funds factories and projects; short-term debt funds daily operations.
terms.how: A sharp rise usually means a big expansion or acquisition is being funded with loans.

terms.meaning: The minimum number of shares you can bid for, and the steps your bid must come in. SEBI sets it so one lot costs roughly ₹10,000 to ₹15,000 on the mainboard.
terms.why: You apply in whole lots, not single shares.
terms.how: Minimum investment = lot size × cap price.

terms.meaning: Investing an amount all at once, instead of in instalments.
terms.why: Money invested earlier has longer to compound, but it all goes in at one price.
terms.how: The two can be combined: a one-time amount at the start plus a monthly SIP.
terms.formula: Future value = Amount × (1 + r)^n
terms.finlit: FinLit's SIP calculator can add a one-time amount on day one.

terms.meaning: The gap between the 12-day and the 26-day EMA of the price. Its own 9-day EMA is the signal line, and the histogram is MACD minus the signal line.
terms.why: It summarises the direction of the trend and whether momentum is picking up or fading.
terms.how: MACD above its signal line with a rising histogram describes strengthening upward momentum. It lags the price and turns often in sideways markets.
terms.formula: MACD = EMA 12 − EMA 26; Signal line = EMA 9 of MACD; Histogram = MACD − Signal line
terms.finlit: FinLit's short-term technical view uses the daily MACD against its signal line and whether the histogram is rising; the long-term view uses the weekly MACD against its signal line and against zero.

terms.meaning: An IPO by a larger company that lists on the main NSE and BSE platforms.
terms.why: Mainboard IPOs follow the full set of SEBI rules on disclosure and investor categories.
terms.how: Most well-known IPOs are mainboard issues.

terms.meaning: A share of revenue kept as profit at some level, such as gross, operating or net margin. In trading, 'margin' can also mean money borrowed from a broker to buy shares.
terms.why: Margins show pricing power and cost control.
terms.how: Always ask 'which margin?' and compare it with the company's own history and its peers.
terms.formula: Net margin % = Net income ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.meaning: How many stocks rose versus fell on a day, for example '91 rose, 424 fell'.
terms.why: It shows whether a move was broad or driven by a few big companies.
terms.how: An index rising while most stocks fall is a narrow, weaker rally.
terms.finlit: On FinLit's sector pages, breadth is the share of an industry's counted stocks above their own 9, 20 and 50-day averages.

terms.meaning: The total market value of a company: share price multiplied by the number of shares.
terms.why: It tells you how big the company is in the stock market's eyes and decides whether it is a large, mid or small cap.
terms.how: ₹16 lakh crore market cap means the market values the whole company at that amount today.
terms.formula: Market cap = Share price × Shares outstanding

terms.meaning: A broker required to quote buy and sell prices in an SME stock for at least three years after listing.
terms.why: It provides some liquidity in small, thinly traded shares.
terms.how: Even with a market maker, SME shares can be hard to sell in size.

terms.meaning: A market order buys or sells straight away at the best price available. A limit order sets the worst price you will accept and waits until it can be filled at that price or better.
terms.why: In fast or thinly traded stocks, market orders can fill at a surprising price.
terms.how: Use limit orders for small companies and in the first minutes of trading.

terms.meaning: The date when a bond, deposit or loan's principal is repaid.
terms.why: It tells you when your money comes back.
terms.how: Match maturities to when you will need the money.

terms.meaning: The strike price at which option buyers, taken together, would receive the smallest total payout if the underlying expired there.
terms.why: Some traders watch it because it marks the level where option sellers as a group would pay out least.
terms.how: There is little evidence that prices are drawn towards it; read it as a description of open positions.
terms.finlit: FinLit works it out from the open interest at every strike of the expiry.

terms.meaning: An open standard that lets AI assistants, such as Claude, ChatGPT or Cursor, call outside data sources. FinLit offers a free, read-only MCP connection to its Indian stock, fund and market data.
terms.why: An assistant connected this way can look up FinLit's figures instead of relying on what it remembers.
terms.how: Check any figure an assistant quotes against the FinLit page; assistants can still misread data.

terms.meaning: India's main commodity derivatives exchange, where futures on gold, silver, crude oil, natural gas and base metals trade.
terms.why: MCX futures prices are the usual Indian reference for commodity prices.
terms.how: A futures price is for a contract month and includes carrying costs; it is not what a jeweller or bank will charge.
terms.finlit: FinLit's commodity page shows the MCX futures price with its contract month, next to the international price in US dollars.

terms.meaning: The middle value when numbers are lined up in order; half are above it and half below.
terms.why: It is less distorted by extreme values than the average.
terms.how: FinLit compares ratios with their 5-year or 8-year median, and companies with the sector median.

terms.meaning: A robust measure of spread: the median of how far each value is from the median. Unlike the standard deviation, one extreme value hardly changes it.
terms.why: It picks out unusual years without letting the unusual year distort the yardstick.
terms.how: A value several MADs from the median is unusual; look for a one-off cause before reading a trend into it.
terms.formula: MAD = Median of |Value − Median|
terms.finlit: In FinLit's ratio tables an 'unusual year' sits far from the row's other years by this measure, and by more than 15% of the median.
aliases: Unusual year: far from this row's other years

terms.meaning: The smallest amount needed to apply: one lot at the upper end of the price band.
terms.why: It tells you whether an IPO fits your budget.
terms.how: Applying for one lot usually gives retail investors the best chance in an oversubscribed IPO, since allotment is by lottery.

terms.meaning: The speed and strength of recent price moves.
terms.why: Stocks that have risen strongly sometimes keep rising for a while, and vice versa.
terms.how: Momentum fades eventually; combine it with fundamentals.

terms.meaning: The six-member committee that sets the RBI's repo rate. It meets at least four times a year, in practice about every two months.
terms.why: Its repo rate decisions move loan rates, deposit rates and bond prices.
terms.how: Read the statement that comes with each decision: the stance it states, such as neutral, shows how the committee sees the outlook.
terms.finlit: FinLit's macro page lists every repo rate decision of the MPC since April 2016.

terms.meaning: The share of months in a period, such as the last 36, in which a fund's return beat the median of its category.
terms.why: It shows whether a fund's lead came steadily or from a few strong months.
terms.how: About half is what chance alone would give; well above half over three years points to steadiness.
terms.formula: Months ahead % = Months above the category median ÷ Months counted × 100
terms.finlit: In FinLit's Mutual Fund Health Score this is 'Months it matched similar funds', part of Performance.

terms.meaning: The average closing price over the last 50 or 200 trading days, redrawn each day. An EMA (exponential moving average) gives recent days more weight.
terms.why: It smooths daily noise to show the trend.
terms.how: Price above its 200-day average is often read as a long-term uptrend; below as a downtrend.
terms.formula: Simple moving average = Sum of last n closes ÷ n
terms.finlit: FinLit uses exponential moving averages (EMA) for its price-against-average figures.

terms.meaning: A fund that pools money from many investors and is managed by a professional fund manager, investing in shares, bonds or both.
terms.why: It offers diversification and professional management for small amounts.
terms.how: Compare funds on long-run returns against their benchmark, costs (expense ratio) and consistency.

terms.meaning: FinLit's 0 to 100 score of a mutual fund against funds of the same kind, built from four parts: Performance, Risk, Cost and Quality (age, size and how the portfolio is built), with weights that depend on the fund group.
terms.why: Return is only one part of a fund; how bumpy and deep its falls were and what it costs count too.
terms.how: Read the group, the rank inside it and the risk-o-meter next to the score: a 75 for a small-cap fund and a 75 for a liquid fund do not mean the same thing. It is not a forecast or advice.
terms.formula: Score = Performance × weight + Risk × weight + Cost × weight + Quality × weight
terms.finlit: Each measure earns 0 points at its worst value and 100 at its best, in a straight line between. Performance is capped at 35% of the score. Direct and Regular plans are scored separately. A fund with 12 to 35 months of NAV history is provisional and its label stops at Healthy; under 12 months it is not rated.

terms.meaning: A company that lends money or provides financial services but does not hold a full banking licence, such as Bajaj Finance.
terms.why: NBFCs cannot take ordinary savings deposits, so they depend more on borrowing.
terms.how: Judge NBFCs on asset quality, funding costs and capital, like banks.

terms.meaning: The value of one unit of a mutual fund, calculated at the end of each business day.
terms.why: You buy and sell units at the NAV.
terms.how: A low NAV does not make a fund cheap; returns depend on growth, not on the starting NAV.
terms.formula: NAV = (Assets − Liabilities) ÷ Units outstanding

terms.meaning: Total debt minus cash and equivalents. A negative figure means net cash.
terms.why: It shows the real debt burden after using available cash.
terms.how: Net debt to EBITDA below about 2 is generally considered comfortable for most industries.
terms.formula: Net debt = Total debt − Cash and equivalents
terms.finlit: FinLit uses borrowings minus the cash and cash equivalents line; investments are not subtracted.

terms.meaning: Net debt divided by yearly EBITDA: roughly how many years of operating profit it would take to repay the debt.
terms.why: Lenders and rating agencies watch it closely.
terms.how: Above 3 to 4 starts to look stretched for most businesses.
terms.formula: Net debt to EBITDA = Net debt ÷ EBITDA

terms.meaning: Profit left after every expense, interest and tax: the 'bottom line'. Often called PAT, profit after tax.
terms.why: It is the profit that belongs to shareholders and the base for EPS and P/E.
terms.how: Check whether net profit is backed by operating cash flow, and whether one-off items inflated it.
terms.formula: Net income = Revenue − All expenses (including interest, depreciation and tax)
terms.finlit: FinLit uses profit attributable to the company's shareholders.

terms.meaning: Net interest income is interest earned on loans minus interest paid on deposits and borrowings. Net interest margin (NIM) is that figure as a share of interest-earning assets.
terms.why: It is a lender's core earnings engine.
terms.how: Indian banks' NIMs are typically about 3–4%; a falling NIM squeezes profit.
terms.formula: NIM % = Net interest income ÷ Average interest-earning assets × 100

terms.meaning: The share of revenue that ends up as net profit after every cost and tax.
terms.why: It shows how much of each ₹100 of sales the shareholders keep.
terms.how: A net margin of 7.5% means ₹7.50 of profit for every ₹100 of sales.
terms.formula: Net margin % = Net profit ÷ Revenue × 100
terms.finlit: The provider's margins are measured against total income (sales plus other income); the statements net margin used by the score and screener divides by sales.
aliases: Net margin change, year on year

terms.meaning: Future cash flows converted into today's money, minus the upfront cost.
terms.why: A rupee next year is worth less than a rupee today; NPV accounts for that.
terms.how: A positive NPV means a project earns more than the required return.
terms.formula: NPV = Sum of CF in year t ÷ (1 + r)^t − Initial investment

terms.meaning: What a person or company owns minus what it owes. For a company it is the same as shareholders' equity.
terms.why: A rising net worth means the owner is getting richer on paper.
terms.how: Track your own net worth once a year: it is a better progress measure than any single investment.
terms.formula: Net worth = Total assets − Total liabilities

terms.meaning: India's two headline indices. The Nifty 50 tracks 50 large companies on the NSE; the Sensex tracks 30 large companies on BSE.
terms.why: When news says 'the market fell 1%', it usually means one of these.
terms.how: Use them as the benchmark for a portfolio of large companies; use midcap or smallcap indices for smaller ones.

terms.meaning: Individuals, companies and trusts applying for more than ₹2 lakh. Split into small NII (₹2 lakh to ₹10 lakh, one third of the portion) and big NII (above ₹10 lakh, two thirds).
terms.why: NII demand often reflects wealthy and leveraged investors chasing listing gains.
terms.how: NII allotment is also by lottery of minimum application size, so applying for more does not guarantee more shares.

terms.meaning: A bond issued by an Indian company that cannot be converted into shares. Reliance, for example, allotted NCDs of ₹1 lakh face value each in October 2026.
terms.why: Companies use NCDs to borrow from investors instead of banks.
terms.how: Higher interest usually means higher risk; read the credit rating.

terms.meaning: Profit with one-off items taken out, and the return on equity worked out from that profit, to show what the business earns in a usual year.
terms.why: A large one-off gain or loss can make one year's profit and ROE misleading.
terms.how: Compare reported and normalized figures: a gap that shows up year after year means the one-offs are not really one-off.
terms.formula: Normalized profit = Reported net profit − One-off items × (1 − Tax rate on one-offs)
terms.finlit: FinLit's Profit Reality Check takes one-off items out after tax, at the tax rate it shows, and works out ROE from the result.

terms.meaning: Operating cash flow as a percentage of revenue: how many rupees of cash the business brings in from each ₹100 of sales.
terms.why: It is harder to dress up than the profit margin, because it counts cash actually received.
terms.how: Compare it with the operating margin over several years; a cash margin well below the profit margin year after year is a warning.
terms.formula: OCF margin % = Operating cash flow ÷ Revenue × 100
terms.finlit: FinLit's earnings and cash checks treat an OCF margin below 5% as weak, or below 3% for project and EPC businesses.

terms.meaning: Existing shareholders, such as promoters or private-equity funds, selling their shares in an IPO. The money goes to them, not the company. Listed companies' promoters can also sell through a special 'OFS window' on the exchanges.
terms.why: A large OFS means early investors are cashing out.
terms.how: An IPO that is mostly OFS raises no new money for the business.

terms.meaning: A running total that adds the day's volume when the price closes up and subtracts it when the price closes down.
terms.why: It shows whether volume has been heavier on rising days or on falling days.
terms.how: OBV rising with the price shows volume behind the move; OBV falling while the price rises is a divergence worth noting.
terms.formula: OBV today = OBV yesterday + Volume (on an up close) or − Volume (on a down close)
terms.finlit: FinLit's 'Volume flow' row scores +1 when OBV is above its 20-day EMA in the short-term view, and when the 50-day EMA of OBV is above its 150-day EMA in the long-term view.

terms.meaning: The number of futures or option contracts that are still open, not yet closed or settled, at the end of a day.
terms.why: Rising open interest means new positions are being opened; falling open interest means positions are being closed.
terms.how: Read the change in open interest with the change in price to see whether positions are being added or cut (see build-up).
terms.formula: OI change = Open interest today − Open interest the day before
terms.finlit: FinLit shows the OI change as a percentage only when the previous day's open interest was above zero.

terms.meaning: An open-ended fund takes in and pays out money every business day at the NAV. A closed-ended fund raises money once, runs for a fixed term and can be sold only on the stock exchange or when it matures. An interval fund opens only at set times.
terms.why: It decides whether and when you can enter or leave. Many closed-ended and interval schemes have stopped publishing NAVs because their term ended.
terms.how: Check the scheme type before assuming you can sell at the NAV on any day.
terms.finlit: FinLit marks closed-ended and interval schemes from AMFI's headings and hides schemes that stopped publishing NAVs unless you ask to see them.

terms.meaning: Cash generated by the main business in a period, after paying suppliers, staff and taxes.
terms.why: It is the clearest sign that a business really earns money.
terms.how: Operating cash flow consistently below net profit needs explaining.

terms.meaning: The share of revenue left after operating costs, before interest and tax.
terms.why: It shows how efficiently the core business runs.
terms.how: A margin rising steadily over several years usually means growing efficiency or pricing power.
terms.formula: Operating margin % = Operating profit ÷ Revenue × 100
terms.finlit: FinLit has two operating margins: the provider's (operating profit − depreciation + other income, over total income) and the statements one (operating profit ÷ sales), which the score and screener use.

terms.meaning: Profit from the core business: revenue minus operating costs, before interest, depreciation, tax and other income. FinLit's P&L shows it this way, which is close to EBITDA.
terms.why: It shows how much the business itself earns, separate from how it is financed.
terms.how: Compare operating profit growth with revenue growth to see whether the business is becoming more or less efficient.

terms.meaning: The value of the best alternative you give up when you choose something.
terms.why: Holding cash or a weak stock has a cost: the return you could have earned elsewhere.
terms.how: Compare every investment with a simple alternative, such as an index fund.
terms.formula: Opportunity cost = Return on best option given up − Return on chosen option

terms.meaning: A contract giving the right, but not the obligation, to buy (call) or sell (put) an asset at a fixed price before expiry.
terms.why: Buyers risk only the price paid; sellers can lose far more.
terms.how: Options lose value as expiry approaches if the price does not move enough.

terms.meaning: A table of all the call and put options on one underlying for an expiry date, strike by strike, with each option's price, open interest, volume and implied volatility.
terms.why: It shows at a glance where positions are concentrated and how options are priced.
terms.how: Calls are usually on the left, strikes in the centre and puts on the right. It describes positions already taken; it does not predict where the price will go.
terms.finlit: FinLit's option chain covers Nifty, Bank Nifty, Sensex and F&O stocks, with OI change, the put-call ratio and max pain.

terms.meaning: Income that does not come from the main business, such as interest on cash, dividends from investments or gains from selling assets.
terms.why: A big jump in other income can make profit look better than the business really is.
terms.how: If other income is a large share of profit before tax, find out whether it will repeat.

terms.meaning: Overbought means the price has risen fast and may pause or pull back; oversold means it has fallen fast and may bounce.
terms.why: They describe short-term mood, not business value.
terms.how: Oversold alone is not a reason to expect a rebound; ask why the stock fell.

terms.meaning: A facility that lets you withdraw more than your account balance, up to a limit, paying interest on what you use.
terms.why: It is flexible short-term credit but usually expensive.
terms.how: Use it for brief gaps, not as long-term borrowing.

terms.meaning: An ETF listed in India that holds shares listed abroad, such as the Nasdaq-100, the S&P 500 or Hang Seng companies.
terms.why: Its value depends on foreign share prices and on the rupee against the foreign currency.
terms.how: Limits on how much money Indian funds may send abroad can make the exchange price differ widely from the NAV; check the premium or discount.

terms.meaning: Oversubscription means bids exceed the shares offered; undersubscription means they fall short.
terms.why: An undersubscribed IPO can fail if it does not reach the minimum required.
terms.how: Weak demand from institutions is a warning sign worth noticing.

terms.meaning: How many days, on average, the company takes to pay its suppliers.
terms.why: Paying later keeps cash in the business longer.
terms.how: Very long payable days can mean the company is short of cash.
terms.formula: Payable days = Payables ÷ Cost of goods sold × 365

terms.meaning: Companies in the same industry used for comparison.
terms.why: Ratios are only meaningful against similar businesses.
terms.how: For companies with several businesses, pick peers for each major segment.

terms.meaning: The P/E ratio divided by the expected or recent EPS growth rate.
terms.why: It adjusts P/E for growth: a high P/E may be fair for a fast grower.
terms.how: As a rough guide, a PEG near 1 is often called fairly priced; it is only as good as the growth figure used.
terms.formula: PEG = P/E ÷ EPS growth rate (%)
terms.finlit: FinLit divides P/E by the 5-year growth in net profit, not EPS growth.

terms.meaning: A percentage point is the plain difference between two percentages: a rise from 10% to 12% is 2 percentage points, but a 20% increase. A basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point.
terms.why: Mixing the two makes changes look bigger or smaller than they are.
terms.how: Rates and shares are usually compared in points: a repo rate cut of 25 bp is 0.25 percentage points.
terms.formula: 1 percentage point = 100 basis points
terms.finlit: FinLit writes 'pts' for percentage points, for example for changes in shareholding.

terms.meaning: A percentile says what share of a group sits below a value: the 90th percentile is higher than 90% of the group. A rank orders the group from first to last.
terms.why: Ranks make figures comparable when their units or spreads differ.
terms.how: Check the group: the top of a weak group can still be weak in absolute terms.
terms.formula: Percentile = Number of values below ÷ Number of values × 100

terms.meaning: Company totals divided by the number of shares: sales per share, cash per share, net cash per share, free cash flow per share.
terms.why: They let you compare a company's numbers directly with its share price.
terms.how: Net cash per share above zero means the company has more cash than debt.

terms.term: Pillars (Quality, Growth, Profitability, Balance sheet, Technical)
terms.meaning: The five areas FinLit IQs. Quality covers returns on capital and how well profit turns into cash; Growth covers sales and profit growth; Profitability covers margins and how hard assets work; Balance sheet covers how much of the assets are funded by liabilities and whether profit is backed by cash; Technical covers the price trend.
terms.why: A stock can be strong in some pillars and weak in others; the pillars show where.
terms.how: Read the pillars before the overall score: a 60 made of 80s and 40s is very different from steady 60s.
aliases: Quality, Growth, Profitability, Balance sheet, Technical

terms.meaning: All the investments a person or institution holds.
terms.why: Judging the whole portfolio matters more than any single holding.
terms.how: Track portfolio-level return, sector mix and score, as FinLit's portfolio page does.

terms.meaning: Preference shares pay a fixed dividend that must be paid before ordinary shareholders get anything, and rank ahead of them if the company is wound up. That fixed payout is the preference dividend.
terms.why: The profit that belongs to ordinary shareholders is net profit minus preference dividends, and that is the figure EPS uses.
terms.how: Few Indian listed companies have them; when one does, take them off net profit before working out EPS.
terms.formula: Profit for ordinary shareholders = Net profit − Preference dividends
terms.finlit: FinLit's EPS calculator has a box for preference dividends, in ₹ crore.

terms.meaning: Shares sold privately to selected investors shortly before the IPO, at a negotiated price.
terms.why: The price shows how insiders value the company just before the offer.
terms.how: A pre-IPO price well below the IPO price raises the question of why the public pays more.

terms.meaning: How far an ETF's exchange price is above (premium) or below (discount) the net asset value of its underlying holdings on the same day.
terms.why: It shows whether people paid more or less on the exchange than the holdings were worth that day.
terms.how: Compare the exchange close and the NAV of the same day only; a NAV for a market holiday has no matching exchange price. Wide gaps are common for ETFs that hold overseas shares.
terms.formula: Premium / discount = (Exchange close ÷ NAV − 1) × 100
terms.finlit: FinLit shows it only when the ETF traded on the day of the NAV published by AMFI.

terms.meaning: Profit before tax as a share of revenue.
terms.why: It includes interest and other income, so it shows the full picture before tax.
terms.how: If pre-tax margin rises while operating margin falls, other income or lower interest is doing the work.
terms.formula: Pre-tax margin % = Profit before tax ÷ Revenue × 100

terms.term: Price band (floor price and cap price)
terms.meaning: The range within which investors may bid in a book-built IPO, such as ₹1,065 to ₹1,119. The lower end is the floor, the upper end the cap.
terms.why: SEBI caps the band so the top is at most 20% above the bottom.
terms.how: Most IPOs end up priced at the cap; plan your application at the upper end.

terms.meaning: A jump in price between two sessions that leaves an empty space on the chart, because the day opened above the previous high or below the previous low. A breakaway gap starts a new move; an exhaustion gap comes late in a long one.
terms.why: Gaps often follow news, and where they come in a trend says something about whether a move is starting or tiring.
terms.how: Gaps on heavy volume carry more weight. Whether a gap was breakaway or exhaustion is often clear only later.
terms.finlit: In FinLit's short-term technical view a breakaway gap up counts +1, an exhaustion gap up −1 and a gap down that closes lower −0.5.

terms.meaning: The change in a price between two dates, as a percentage, without adding dividends or other payouts received in between.
terms.why: It is the simplest measure of how a price moved, but it understates what a holder received when the fund pays out income.
terms.how: Funds that pay out their income, such as many liquid ETFs, can show a price return near zero while holders still received money. Total return adds those payouts.
terms.formula: Price return = (Latest price ÷ Earlier price − 1) × 100
terms.finlit: Every return on FinLit's ETF pages is a price return.

terms.term: Price to cash flow and price to free cash flow
terms.meaning: Market cap divided by yearly operating cash flow (P/CFO) or by free cash flow (P/FCF).
terms.why: Cash is harder to dress up than profit, so these ratios can be more reliable than P/E.
terms.how: If P/FCF is far higher than P/E, profits are not turning into spare cash.
terms.formula: P/FCF = Market cap ÷ Free cash flow

terms.meaning: The share price divided by book value per share: what you pay for each rupee of net assets.
terms.why: Most useful for banks, insurers and asset-heavy companies, whose assets are close to their real value.
terms.how: A P/B below 1 means the market values the company below its book value; find out why before calling it cheap.
terms.formula: P/B = Share price ÷ Book value per share

terms.meaning: The share price divided by EPS: how many rupees investors pay for each rupee of yearly profit.
terms.why: It is the quickest way to judge whether a stock is cheap or expensive relative to its profits.
terms.how: Compare P/E with the company's own history and its industry. A low P/E can mean cheap, or it can mean the market expects profits to fall.
terms.formula: P/E = Share price ÷ EPS
terms.finlit: FinLit recalculates the provider's P/E at the latest price and leaves it blank when profit is not positive.

terms.meaning: Market cap divided by yearly revenue.
terms.why: Useful for young or loss-making companies that have no profit to put in a P/E.
terms.how: Compare only within an industry; high-margin businesses naturally trade at higher P/S.
terms.formula: P/S = Market cap ÷ Revenue

terms.meaning: The primary market is where new shares are first sold, as in an IPO. The secondary market is the stock exchange, where investors trade existing shares with each other.
terms.why: In the primary market your money goes to the company or selling shareholders; in the secondary market it goes to another investor.
terms.how: After listing, an IPO share trades like any other in the secondary market.

terms.meaning: The original amount borrowed or invested, not counting interest or returns.
terms.why: Interest is calculated on the principal (and, with compounding, on past interest).
terms.how: Prepaying part of a loan reduces the principal and the interest that follows.
terms.formula: Simple interest = P × R × T ÷ 100

terms.meaning: The report of a company's income and costs over a period, ending in its profit. Also called the income statement.
terms.why: It answers 'did the business make money this year or quarter, and how?'
terms.how: Read it top to bottom: revenue, minus costs, gives operating profit; then interest, depreciation and tax lead to net profit.

terms.meaning: Profit after all expenses, interest and depreciation, but before income tax.
terms.why: It allows comparisons between companies that pay different tax rates.
terms.how: Divide PBT by revenue to get the pre-tax margin.

terms.meaning: A section of FinLit's company report that tests how far profit and ROE reflect the business: one-off items, normalized profit and ROE, the DuPont breakdown and whether profit is backed by cash.
terms.why: Headline profit can flatter or hide what the business really earns.
terms.how: Read it before relying on a high ROE or a sudden jump in profit.

terms.meaning: The founders, family or parent company that control a listed company.
terms.why: Promoters usually decide strategy, so their track record and conduct matter.
terms.how: High, stable promoter holding generally means the owners stay committed; steady selling deserves questions.

terms.meaning: Promoter holding is the share of the company the promoter group owns. A pledge is when promoters use their shares as security for a loan.
terms.why: If the share price falls, lenders can sell pledged shares, pushing the price down further.
terms.how: A rising pledged share is a classic warning sign.

terms.meaning: The final offer document, filed after the price is fixed, with the issue price and final size.
terms.why: It is the legal record of what was offered.
terms.how: Keep it for reference after listing; it lists lock-ins and promised uses of money.

terms.meaning: The share of bad loans a bank has already set money aside for.
terms.why: Higher coverage means less risk of future hits to profit.
terms.how: Above about 70% is generally considered comfortable.

terms.meaning: A FinLit Prism rating given on less evidence than a full one: coverage is between 50% and 80%, or there are fewer than six comparable quarters to judge the sales and profit record. A provisional rating is never higher than Healthy.
terms.why: It still shows the score, while making clear that it rests on incomplete data.
terms.how: Read it as a first view and look at what is missing. When coverage is below 50%, the income history is too short or the industry group cannot be identified, Prism says Not rated and gives no score.

terms.meaning: A short fall within a larger uptrend, or a short rise within a downtrend, before the main trend carries on.
terms.why: It separates a pause in a trend from a change of direction.
terms.how: A pullback that breaks below the rising moving averages may be more than a pause.
terms.finlit: FinLit's short-term technical view looks for an uptrend (close above EMA 50, with EMA 9 above 20 above 50) and a close within 2% above EMA 9.

terms.meaning: Total open interest in put options divided by total open interest in call options, across every strike of an expiry. PCR by volume uses the day's traded volume instead.
terms.why: It sums up how positions are split between puts and calls.
terms.how: It is a ratio of positions, not a forecast: the same PCR can come from hedging or from bets on a fall.
terms.formula: PCR = Total put open interest ÷ Total call open interest

terms.meaning: The chance of seeing a link at least as strong as the one measured if there were in fact no link at all. A small p-value means the pattern is unlikely to be pure chance.
terms.why: With few points, strong-looking patterns appear by luck; the p-value puts a number on that.
terms.how: Below 0.05 is the usual line for 'statistically significant'. A significant link can still be too small to matter, and testing many pairs turns some up by luck.
terms.finlit: FinLit's correlation charts draw a regression line only when the link passes statistical tests.

terms.meaning: Large professional investors such as mutual funds, banks, insurance companies, pension funds and registered foreign portfolio investors.
terms.why: Their demand is watched as a sign of professional confidence.
terms.how: Strong QIB subscription is not a guarantee: institutions also misjudge prices.

terms.meaning: A quick way for a listed company to raise money by selling new shares only to qualified institutional buyers.
terms.why: It raises capital faster than a public offer.
terms.how: A QIP at a discount to the market price can weigh on the share price briefly.

terms.meaning: A central bank buying large amounts of government bonds or other securities to push money into the economy and lower long-term interest rates.
terms.why: QE by large central banks affects global money flows, including into Indian markets.
terms.how: Watch for it in global news; foreign investor flows often follow.

terms.meaning: Where a stock's 6-month return ranks among the counted stocks of its industry: top quarter, 2nd, 3rd or bottom quarter.
terms.why: It places a stock's recent price move against its industry peers.
terms.how: It describes the past. In FinLit's study, the median stock in every quarter still trailed the industry index after a C thrust.

terms.meaning: Financial results listed companies publish every three months, within 45 days of the quarter's end (60 days for the full year).
terms.why: They are the most frequent official update on how a business is doing.
terms.how: Compare a quarter with the same quarter a year earlier, because many businesses are seasonal.

terms.meaning: The change in a figure compared with the immediately preceding quarter.
terms.why: It shows the latest direction, but it is affected by seasons.
terms.how: A strong QoQ jump in a seasonal business may just be the festive quarter.
aliases: Operating profit growth, quarter on quarter

terms.meaning: A FinLit tool where you type a screening rule, such as Market cap > 500 AND P/E < 15, and get every listed Indian company that matches.
terms.why: It allows rules a menu of filters cannot, such as comparing one ratio with another.
terms.how: Amounts are in ₹ crore. Use brackets to group OR conditions, and save a query as a basket to run it again later.

terms.meaning: Like the current ratio but leaving out inventory, which may be slow to sell.
terms.why: It is a stricter test of whether bills can be paid quickly.
terms.how: A quick ratio near or above 1 means short-term bills are covered without selling stock.
terms.formula: Quick ratio = (Current assets − Inventory) ÷ Current liabilities

terms.meaning: An interest rate minus inflation.
terms.why: It shows whether borrowing is really costly once rising prices are allowed for: below zero, prices rise faster than the rate.
terms.how: A positive real rate tends to slow borrowing and spending; a negative one tends to encourage them.
terms.formula: Real rate ≈ Nominal rate − Inflation
terms.finlit: FinLit's macro page uses the repo rate minus CPI inflation.

terms.meaning: The profit or loss on investments you have actually sold, from the buying and selling prices. Gross P&L is before charges and taxes; net P&L is after them.
terms.why: Only realised gains are taxed, and only they turn into cash.
terms.how: Read realised and unrealised figures together: selling winners while keeping losers flatters realised P&L.
terms.formula: Realised P&L = (Sell price − Buy price) × Quantity − Charges
terms.finlit: FinLit's portfolio report shows realised P&L from the broker's statement, after all charges.

terms.meaning: Bringing a portfolio back to its target mix by trimming what has grown and adding to what has shrunk.
terms.why: It controls risk by trimming what has risen and adding to what has fallen.
terms.how: Rebalance on a schedule (yearly) or when a weight drifts by more than about 5 percentage points.

terms.meaning: A way to chart several series from the same starting point: each is divided by its own first value and multiplied by 100. A reading of 130 means a 30% rise since the start.
terms.why: It lets you compare how a ₹50 share and a ₹5,000 share, or two funds, have moved.
terms.how: The start date matters: move it and the picture can change.
terms.formula: Rebased value = Value ÷ First value × 100

terms.meaning: The date on which you must be on the company's list of shareholders to receive a dividend, bonus or split.
terms.why: Because of T+1 settlement, you must buy at least one working day before the record date.
terms.how: Look for the ex-date, which is now usually the same as the record date; buying on or after it means no dividend.

terms.meaning: FinLit screener filters for warning signs: loss-making, negative operating cash flow, profit not backed by cash, high debt, weak interest cover, profit falling sharply, promoters selling and a price far below its long-term trend.
terms.why: Avoiding obvious problems prevents many investing mistakes.
terms.how: Use the red-flag filters as a first check on any stock you are researching.

terms.meaning: Release of blocked money for shares not allotted.
terms.why: With ASBA, nothing is debited, so the block is simply lifted.
terms.how: If funds are still blocked after T+2, contact your bank and the registrar.

terms.meaning: The firm that processes IPO applications, decides allotment under SEBI rules and handles refunds.
terms.why: It is where you check allotment status and raise complaints.
terms.how: The RHP names the registrar.

terms.meaning: The straight line that best fits a scatter of points. The slope is how much Y changes for each 1-unit rise in X; the intercept is the value of Y where the line crosses X = 0.
terms.why: It turns a cloud of points into one readable relationship.
terms.how: Read the slope with R² and the p-value: a steep line through scattered points explains little. One influential point can tilt the line, so check whether leaving it out changes the result.
terms.formula: Y = Intercept + Slope × X
terms.finlit: FinLit's correlation charts also name the most influential point and run a curvature test before deciding whether to draw the line.

terms.meaning: The version of a mutual fund bought through a distributor or advisor. A commission for them is paid out of the fund, so its yearly cost is higher than the Direct plan's.
terms.why: The extra cost lowers the Regular plan's NAV growth against the Direct plan of the same fund, by about the difference in their expense ratios.
terms.how: Compare Regular with Regular, and keep in mind what the extra cost pays for (advice or service).
terms.finlit: On FinLit every scheme shows its plan, and the other plans of the same fund are linked on its page.

terms.meaning: A disclosure made under Regulation 30 of SEBI's listing rules (LODR), which requires companies to report material events promptly.
terms.why: It covers events that could move the share price: big orders, acquisitions, defaults, litigation, management exits.
terms.how: The headline is often generic; open the attached document to see what the event actually is.

terms.meaning: A share's return minus the return of an index over the same period, in percentage points. Positive means the share did better than the index. It is different from RSI.
terms.why: It separates what the share did from what the whole market or sector did.
terms.how: Pick a fitting yardstick: the sector index for sector peers, a size index for size. Past relative strength describes the past and can reverse.
terms.formula: Relative return = Share's return − Index return
terms.finlit: FinLit's technical views rank the share's beta-adjusted return above the index over 21 and 63 days (short term) and 63 to 252 days (long term); the Leader label uses 3, 6 and 12-month returns against the sector index.

terms.meaning: Comparing a company's valuation ratio with its own past (for example its 5-year median P/E) or with the median of its sector.
terms.why: A ratio means little alone; context shows whether it is high or low.
terms.how: Trading below its own 5-year median P/E can mean the shares are priced lower than usual, or that growth has slowed. Check why.

terms.meaning: The interest rate at which the Reserve Bank of India lends short-term money to banks. It is the RBI's main policy rate.
terms.why: Changes ripple into loan rates, deposit rates, bond prices and share valuations.
terms.how: Rate cuts usually help banks' borrowers, real estate and rate-sensitive stocks; hikes do the opposite.

terms.meaning: The results season is the few weeks after each quarter ends, when most listed companies report. The results calendar lists the board-meeting dates companies have announced for approving their results.
terms.why: Prices often move most around results, and knowing the date helps you be ready to read the numbers.
terms.how: Listed companies must publish quarterly results within 45 days of the quarter's end, and the year's audited results within 60 days.
terms.finlit: FinLit's results calendar is built from companies' board-meeting announcements, with recently declared results and their filings.

terms.meaning: Individuals and other non-institutional holders, grouped as 'public' in the shareholding pattern.
terms.why: A rising retail share with falling institutional holding can mean professionals are selling to individuals.
terms.how: Compare the retail trend with institutional trends.

terms.meaning: Profit a company has kept over the years instead of paying it out as dividends.
terms.why: Kept profit funds growth without new borrowing or new shares.
terms.how: Retained profit is only useful if the company earns a good return on it; check ROE alongside.
terms.formula: Retained earnings = Opening balance + Net income − Dividends

terms.meaning: The share of profit kept in the business rather than paid out.
terms.why: Retained profit funds future growth.
terms.how: Retention only helps owners if the company earns a good return (ROE) on what it keeps.
terms.formula: Retention ratio % = 100 − Payout ratio %

terms.meaning: Net profit earned for every ₹100 of assets the company owns.
terms.why: It is especially useful for banks and other lenders, whose assets are mostly loans.
terms.how: For banks, an ROA above about 1% is generally considered good.
terms.formula: ROA % = Net profit ÷ Total assets × 100
terms.finlit: FinLit divides net profit by total assets at the year end.

terms.meaning: Operating profit (EBIT) earned for every ₹100 of total capital used in the business, from both shareholders and lenders.
terms.why: Unlike ROE, it cannot be boosted by borrowing, so it is a fairer test of the business itself.
terms.how: A ROCE consistently above the cost of borrowing (roughly 10–12% in India) suggests the business creates value.
terms.formula: ROCE % = EBIT ÷ (Shareholders' equity + Debt) × 100
terms.finlit: FinLit shows the provider's return on capital. Where none is sent, FinLit uses EBIT ÷ (total assets − current liabilities), not equity plus debt as above.

terms.meaning: How much profit a company makes for every ₹100 its shareholders have put in and left in the business.
terms.why: It shows whether owners' money is being used well; a business that earns more on each rupee can grow without asking for more.
terms.how: Compare with peers and the company's own past. Check debt too: borrowing can push ROE up.
terms.formula: ROE % = Net profit ÷ Average shareholders' equity × 100
terms.finlit: FinLit shows the data provider's ROE: net profit ÷ shareholders' equity at the year end, not the average of two years.

terms.meaning: The gain or loss on an investment as a share of what it cost.
terms.why: It is the simplest way to say how well any investment did.
terms.how: ROI ignores time: 20% over one year is far better than 20% over five. Use CAGR or XIRR to compare across periods.
terms.formula: ROI % = Net gain ÷ Cost of investment × 100

terms.meaning: Net profit as a share of physical and financial assets, leaving out goodwill and other intangibles.
terms.why: It removes the effect of past acquisitions, which inflate assets with goodwill.
terms.how: Use it alongside ROA when a company has bought many businesses.
terms.formula: Return on tangible assets % = Net profit ÷ (Total assets − Intangible assets) × 100

terms.meaning: The money a company earns from selling its goods or services before any costs are taken out. Also called sales, turnover or the 'top line'.
terms.why: Growth in revenue is the starting point for growth in profit.
terms.how: Check whether growth comes from selling more or from charging more, and whether it lasts several years.

terms.meaning: A DCF run backwards: it starts from today's share price and works out the growth that price implies.
terms.why: It turns a hard question (what is it worth?) into one you can judge: is that growth realistic?
terms.how: Compare the implied growth with the company's past growth and with its industry's.
terms.finlit: FinLit's DCF calculator shows a reverse DCF next to the forward calculation; the EPS calculator shows the growth a target price needs.

terms.meaning: The updated offer document filed before the IPO opens, with almost everything except the final price and number of shares.
terms.why: It is the document you are expected to read before applying.
terms.how: Compare it with the DRHP to see what changed.

terms.meaning: An offer to existing shareholders to buy new shares, usually at a discount, in proportion to what they already hold.
terms.why: If you do not take up or sell your rights, your stake is diluted.
terms.how: Rights entitlements can be traded on the exchange for a few days.

terms.meaning: An individual applying for up to ₹2 lakh in an IPO.
terms.why: Retail investors get a large reserved portion and can bid at the cut-off price.
terms.how: When the retail portion is oversubscribed, a lottery decides who gets the minimum lot.

terms.meaning: How much risk you can and are willing to take, based on your age, income, goals, time horizon and temperament.
terms.why: It decides a sensible asset allocation for you.
terms.how: Revisit it when your life changes: marriage, children, a new job, nearing retirement.

terms.meaning: The return on an investment considered to carry almost no risk, usually the yield on Indian government Treasury bills or bonds.
terms.why: It is the minimum any risky investment should beat.
terms.how: Use the current 91-day T-bill or 10-year government bond yield as a reference.

terms.meaning: SEBI's six-level label of a mutual fund's risk, from Low to Very High, which every fund must show and review each month, next to the risk-o-meter of its benchmark.
terms.why: It gives a quick, standard sense of how much a fund's value can swing and how much credit and liquidity risk it takes.
terms.how: Compare it with your own risk profile and with the benchmark's level. It describes the portfolio today, not what will happen.

terms.meaning: A way of fitting a line that takes the median of the slopes between every pair of points instead of using least squares. A few extreme points barely move it.
terms.why: Financial data often has outliers, such as a one-off year, which can tilt an ordinary regression line.
terms.how: If the Theil-Sen slope and the ordinary slope differ a lot, a few points are driving the ordinary line.
terms.formula: Theil-Sen slope = Median of (Yj − Yi) ÷ (Xj − Xi) over all pairs of points

terms.meaning: Returns measured over every window of a fixed length, for example every one-year period ending on each day, instead of over a single start and end date.
terms.why: A single period can flatter or punish a fund depending on the start date; rolling returns show the range of results.
terms.how: Look at the worst window and the share of windows with a gain, not only the average.
terms.finlit: FinLit's ETF and fund pages show the lowest, median and highest one-year window, and the share of windows with a gain.

terms.term: Rotation corners (Ahead and gaining, Ahead but slowing, Behind and slipping, Behind but gaining)
terms.meaning: Where an industry sits on two numbers measured against the average industry: its 6-month return (ahead or behind) and its last month's return (gaining or slowing).
terms.why: Together they show the size of a lead and its direction.
terms.how: A group moves to a new corner only after two weekly readings there, so corners change slowly. In FinLit's 2017–2026 study, Behind but gaining was usually a bounce: 72% of moves out of it went back to Behind and slipping.
terms.formula: Strength = the group's 6-month return − the average industry's 6-month return; Change = the same over the last month (21 sessions)
terms.finlit: Readings are taken at each week's last session; the current week uses its latest session.

terms.meaning: A weekly 0–100 score that ranks NSE industry groups by how far they have run ahead of the average industry over 3, 6 and 12 months, with breadth added.
terms.why: It puts every group on one list, and its weekly moves show which groups are climbing or falling.
terms.how: A rank describes past returns. In FinLit's study the top third did 2.8 points better than the bottom third over the next 3 months, but the gap was close to zero in 2025 and 2026.
terms.formula: Score = 75% × (0.3 × rank of the 3-month + 0.4 × rank of the 6-month + 0.3 × rank of the 12-month return against the average industry) + 25% × rank of breadth (share above the 50-day average); each rank is a percentile across groups
terms.finlit: Each group shows the places it moved in 1 week and in 4 weeks; moves of 3 places or more are highlighted.

terms.meaning: A 0–100 gauge of how strongly a stock has risen versus fallen over the last 14 days.
terms.why: It flags when moves look stretched.
terms.how: Above 70 is usually called overbought, below 30 oversold. Strong trends can stay overbought or oversold for weeks.

terms.meaning: The share of the ups and downs in one measure that a straight line through another measure accounts for, from 0% to 100%. For a simple line it equals the correlation squared.
terms.why: It shows how much a fitted line actually explains, and how much is left unexplained.
terms.how: An R² of 0.2 means the line explains a fifth of the variation; most of the movement comes from other things.
terms.formula: R² = 1 − (Sum of squared residuals ÷ Total sum of squares)

terms.meaning: Revenue or net profit divided by the number of employees.
terms.why: A simple productivity measure.
terms.how: Useful within an industry, such as comparing IT services firms; meaningless across very different industries.

terms.meaning: How fast revenue and net profit have grown, usually shown for the last year and as 3-year and 5-year CAGRs.
terms.why: Profit growing faster than sales means margins are widening; slower means they are shrinking.
terms.how: Check both 3-year and 5-year rates. If they differ a lot, one of the start years was unusual.
aliases: Gap between sales and profit growth

terms.term: Scenario analysis (bear, base and bull cases)
terms.meaning: Working out a value or result under several sets of assumptions, such as a bear, a base and a bull case, sometimes with a probability for each to give a weighted figure.
terms.why: One number hides how much the answer depends on the assumptions.
terms.how: Make the cases genuinely different. A weighted value is only as good as the probabilities put on it.
terms.formula: Weighted value = Sum of (Case value × Probability)
terms.finlit: FinLit's EPS calculator works out Bear, Base and Bull cases, and its DCF calculator can weight cases by the probability you give each.

terms.meaning: FinLit's labels for score ranges: Strong 78 and above, Healthy 62 to 77, Mixed 45 to 61, Watch below 45.
terms.why: Bands make scores easier to read at a glance.
terms.how: A move from one band to another is a reason to look again, not an instruction.

terms.meaning: A tool that lists every company matching rules you set, such as 'P/E below 20 and ROE above 15%'.
terms.why: It narrows thousands of companies to a short list in seconds.
terms.how: Start with a few rules about quality, then add valuation; too many rules leave nothing.

terms.meaning: The Securities and Exchange Board of India: the government body that regulates stock markets, brokers, mutual funds, research analysts and investment advisers.
terms.why: SEBI's rules decide how IPOs work, what companies must disclose and who may give paid investment advice.
terms.how: Before paying anyone for stock tips or advice, check whether they are SEBI-registered.

terms.meaning: A sector is a broad part of the economy, such as Financial Services or Energy. An industry is a narrower group inside it, such as Private Sector Bank or Refineries & Marketing.
terms.why: Companies in the same industry face similar demand, costs and rules, so their numbers can be compared fairly.
terms.how: Judge a ratio against the company's industry, not the whole market: a bank's debt looks nothing like a software firm's.

terms.meaning: An ETF that follows an index of one sector, such as banks or IT, or one theme, such as defence or manufacturing.
terms.why: It puts all of its money into one part of the market, so it moves with that part.
terms.how: Compare it with a broad index ETF to see how much of its movement came from that one sector.

terms.meaning: Industries taking turns to lead the market. FinLit measures it against the average industry: every NSE industry or sector group with a reading, weighted equally.
terms.why: It shows which industries have been pulling ahead of the rest and which have been falling behind, and whether that is speeding up or slowing down.
terms.how: It describes the past. In FinLit's 2017–2026 study the pattern held in equal-weighted industry groups but not in NSE's size-weighted sector indices, and it was weaker when the Nifty 50 was below its 200-day exponential average.
terms.finlit: The Rotation tab on Sector Pulse places each group in one of four corners and ranks the groups every week.

terms.term: Sector signal states (Washout, Thrust, Confirmed, Fading)
terms.meaning: FinLit's labels for where an NSE industry stands in its breadth cycle: Washout (broad selling), Thrust (a broad rebound), Confirmed (most stocks trending up together) and Fading (breadth breaking down).
terms.why: They show whether a move in an industry is broad or narrow, and how it has developed.
terms.how: Read them with the market: is the Nifty 50 above or below its 200-day exponential average? In FinLit's 2017–2026 study many thrusts faded, and averaged week by week their edge was about zero.
terms.finlit: Washout: at some point in the last 30 sessions fewer than 40% of counted stocks were above their 50-day average. Confirmed: 70% or more are above all three averages (9, 20 and 50-day). Fading: a thrust failed, or breadth broke after Confirmed; it lasts 20 sessions or until a new thrust.

terms.meaning: Equity funds that invest at least 80% in one sector, such as banking or pharma, or one theme, such as defence, technology or consumption.
terms.why: They concentrate on one area, so their returns can be far above or far below the broad market for years.
terms.how: Count them as a concentrated position when you look at your overall mix.

terms.term: Sectoral index (Nifty Bank, Nifty IT and others)
terms.meaning: An index that tracks the shares of one sector or theme, such as Nifty Bank, Nifty IT, Nifty Pharma or Nifty Auto.
terms.why: It is the fair yardstick for a company: a bank's year looks different against Nifty Bank than against the Nifty 50.
terms.how: A few large companies can dominate a sector index; check its top weights.
terms.finlit: FinLit's Leader label compares a share with its sector index, such as Nifty IT for IT or Nifty PSU Bank for PSU banks.

terms.meaning: The umbrella word for financial instruments that can be bought and sold: shares, bonds, mutual fund units and derivatives.
terms.why: Rules made by SEBI, the market regulator, apply to all securities, which protects buyers.
terms.how: When a document mentions 'securities', it means any of these tradable instruments, not only shares.

terms.meaning: The breakdown of revenue and profit by business line or region, such as Oil-to-Chemicals, Retail and Digital for Reliance.
terms.why: It shows which parts of a company are growing and which drag it down.
terms.how: A company is often valued as the sum of its segments; check which ones drive profit, not just revenue.

terms.meaning: A table that shows how a result changes as one or two inputs change, such as the value per share for each pair of discount rate and growth rate.
terms.why: It shows which assumptions the answer depends on most.
terms.how: If the value swings from far below to far above the price across reasonable inputs, the calculation cannot settle the question on its own.
terms.finlit: FinLit's DCF and EPS calculators each show a sensitivity grid.

terms.meaning: The process of handing over shares and money after a trade. In India most trades settle one working day after the trade date (T+1).
terms.why: Shares bought today reach your demat account the next working day.
terms.how: Dividend and bonus eligibility depends on settlement, which is why record dates and ex-dates differ (see Record date).

terms.meaning: A portion reserved for shareholders of a listed parent or group company, usually up to 10% of the issue. Insurers sometimes reserve a policyholder portion in the same way.
terms.why: It gives existing investors of the group a better chance of allotment.
terms.how: Check the RHP for the eligibility cut-off date: you must hold the parent's shares by then.

terms.meaning: The quarterly breakdown of who owns a company's shares: promoters, foreign institutions, domestic institutions, government and the public.
terms.why: Changes show who is buying and who is selling.
terms.how: Look at the trend across several quarters, not one quarter's change.

terms.meaning: Return earned above the risk-free rate for each unit of volatility.
terms.why: It compares how well different investments reward you for the risk taken.
terms.how: Higher is better; compare funds or portfolios over the same period.
terms.formula: Sharpe = (Return − Risk-free rate) ÷ Standard deviation
aliases: Return for each unit of price swing

terms.meaning: Interest calculated only on the original principal.
terms.why: It grows in a straight line, unlike compound interest.
terms.how: Most loans and deposits in India compound, so check which applies.
terms.formula: SI = P × R × T ÷ 100

terms.meaning: Investing a fixed amount at regular intervals, usually monthly, in a mutual fund.
terms.why: It builds discipline and averages your buying price over time.
terms.how: Measure SIP returns with XIRR, not simple percentage gain.

terms.meaning: An IPO by a small or medium company that lists on a separate platform, NSE Emerge or BSE SME.
terms.why: Rules are lighter and companies are smaller, so risk is higher and shares can be hard to sell.
terms.how: Minimum application amounts are much larger than on the mainboard; read the offer document carefully.

terms.meaning: A SEBI category of funds built around a goal, retirement funds and children's funds, with a lock-in of at least five years or until retirement age or the child comes of age, whichever is earlier.
terms.why: The lock-in keeps the money invested for the goal.
terms.how: Judge it on what it actually holds, which can range from mostly equity to mostly debt, and on its costs.

terms.meaning: A company's ability to meet all its long-term obligations and keep operating.
terms.why: Solvency problems lead to defaults and, in India, to insolvency proceedings under the IBC.
terms.how: Judge it with debt ratios, interest coverage and cash flow together.

terms.meaning: A price-discovery session on listing day, when orders are collected and a fair opening price is set before normal trading usually begins at 10 am.
terms.why: It reduces wild swings at the open.
terms.how: The opening price is the result of this session, not the issue price.

terms.meaning: A chart with one spoke per measure, each running from weaker at the centre to stronger at the edge, joined into a shape. Several companies can be drawn on top of each other.
terms.why: It shows at a glance where one company is stronger or weaker than another across many measures.
terms.how: Compare spoke by spoke rather than by area, because the area changes with the order of the spokes. Check how each spoke is scaled.

terms.meaning: A way of describing where a share is in its price cycle using a long moving average: Stage 1 basing (the average flat), Stage 2 advancing (price above a rising average), Stage 3 topping (flat again after a rise) and Stage 4 declining (price below a falling average).
terms.why: It places today's price in the longer cycle.
terms.how: Stages are clearer in hindsight than as they happen, and a share can move back and forth between them.
terms.finlit: FinLit reads the stage from the slope of the 150-day average (flat within ±1.5%) and the close against it. Stage 2 counts +1 when fresh and +0.5 when established; in Stage 3 or 4 the long-term score is capped at +19.

terms.meaning: A measure of how spread out values are around their average. In a roughly bell-shaped spread, about two-thirds of values lie within one standard deviation of the average.
terms.why: It is the basic yardstick of variability, behind volatility, tracking error and the Sharpe ratio.
terms.how: Compare standard deviations only for figures in the same unit and period: a yearly figure from daily returns is the daily one × √252.
terms.formula: Standard deviation = √(Average of (Value − Mean)²)

terms.meaning: A SIP whose instalment rises each year, by a fixed amount or a percentage, for example in line with pay rises.
terms.why: Raising the instalment over time can make a large difference to the final value.
terms.how: A 10% yearly step-up on ₹10,000 a month means ₹11,000 a month in the second year.
terms.formula: Instalment in year n = First instalment × (1 + Step-up %)^(n − 1)

terms.meaning: A regulated marketplace where buyers and sellers trade securities. India's two main exchanges are the National Stock Exchange (NSE) and BSE (formerly the Bombay Stock Exchange).
terms.why: The exchange matches orders, publishes prices and makes listed companies file results and news publicly.
terms.how: Most large companies trade on both. FinLit shows each company's NSE symbol and BSE code.
