terms.meaning: A small piece of ownership in a company. Owning one share of a company with 100 crore shares means you own one part in 100 crore of it.
terms.why: Shareholders gain when the company's value rises and may receive part of its profit as dividends.
terms.how: Think of a share as a slice of a business, not a lottery ticket: its long-run value follows the company's profits.

terms.meaning: Dividing each share into smaller units, for example one ₹10 share into five ₹2 shares. The price per share falls in proportion.
terms.why: It makes shares cheaper to buy in small amounts; the value of your holding stays the same.
terms.how: Charts and per-share figures must be adjusted for splits to be compared over time.

terms.meaning: An order that sells automatically if the price falls to a level you choose.
terms.why: It limits how much you can lose on a trade if you cannot watch the screen.
terms.how: Set it below normal day-to-day swings, or ordinary noise will trigger it.

terms.meaning: Plain-language findings FinLit draws from a company's numbers, such as 'profit backed by cash' or 'price below its long-term trend'.
terms.why: They point to what deserves a closer look.
terms.how: Check the period each finding covers before relying on it.

terms.meaning: The price at which an option lets its buyer buy the underlying (a call) or sell it (a put).
terms.why: The strike, against the current price, decides whether an option has any value if exercised now.
terms.how: The at-the-money strike is the one nearest the current price.
terms.finlit: FinLit marks the listed strike nearest the underlying's last price; exactly midway between two, the higher one.

terms.meaning: How much demand there was compared with shares on offer. '25 times subscribed' means bids for 25 times the shares available.
terms.why: It shows interest from each investor category.
terms.how: High subscription raises the chance of listing gains but lowers your chance of allotment.

terms.meaning: A company controlled by another (its parent), usually through owning more than half its shares.
terms.why: A parent's consolidated results include its subsidiaries.
terms.how: When a subsidiary lists through an IPO, the parent's shareholders may see value unlocked.

terms.meaning: When the price pushes past a recent swing high or swing low but cannot hold there and closes back inside the earlier range.
terms.why: It shows an attempt to break out that did not stick.
terms.how: Treat it as a description of a failed attempt, not as a signal on its own.
terms.finlit: FinLit's short-term technical view counts an active bullish swing failure +0.75 (+1 once confirmed) and a bearish one −0.75 (−1 once confirmed); the long-term view uses 15-session swings.

terms.meaning: The short code a stock trades under, such as RELIANCE on the NSE, and the six-digit number BSE uses, such as 500325.
terms.why: Codes avoid confusion between companies with similar names.
terms.how: Search FinLit with either the name, the NSE symbol or the BSE code.

terms.meaning: IPO shares must list within three working days after the issue closes (T). Allotment is finalised on T+1, shares are credited and unused money unblocked on T+2, and listing happens on T+3.
terms.why: Your money is blocked for only a few days.
terms.how: Mark T+3 in your calendar as the listing day.

terms.meaning: The price-to-earnings multiple you assume the shares will trade at at the end of a scenario, used to turn a projected EPS into a price.
terms.why: The future price in a scenario depends as much on this assumed multiple as on EPS growth.
terms.how: Try several values: the sensitivity grid shows how the result moves. A multiple is an assumption, not a prediction.
terms.formula: Implied future price = Future EPS × Target P/E

terms.meaning: An amount you can subtract from income before tax is calculated, such as Section 80C investments under the old tax regime.
terms.why: Deductions reduce taxable income and therefore tax.
terms.how: Compare the old and new tax regimes each year; the new one offers fewer deductions but lower rates.
terms.formula: Taxable income = Gross income − Deductions

terms.meaning: Tax withheld by the payer, such as a company paying dividends or a bank paying interest, and paid to the government on your behalf.
terms.why: It shows up in your Form 26AS and annual information statement.
terms.how: Claim TDS as already paid when you file your return.

terms.meaning: Studying price and trading volume to judge trends and momentum, rather than studying the business itself (fundamental analysis).
terms.why: Price behaviour shows what buyers and sellers are doing right now.
terms.how: FinLit keeps the technical score separate from the Growth & Profitability score so you can read each on its own.

terms.meaning: FinLit's two price-trend scores: a short-term view of recent weeks and a long-term view of the past year. Trend alignment puts the two together in plain words, such as 'Rising on both', 'Dip in an uptrend' or 'Falling on both'.
terms.why: A short dip inside a long uptrend reads differently from a fall inside a long downtrend.
terms.how: The labels describe past prices only; they do not predict and are not advice. Read them next to the business scores.
terms.finlit: Each score counts as up at +20 or more, down at −20 or less and sideways in between, and the nine combinations give the labels. The short-term view uses daily EMAs, MACD, RSI, volume and price patterns; the long-term view uses the 200-day trend, weekly RSI and MACD, relative strength and the stage.

terms.meaning: In a DCF, the value of all the cash flows after the forecast years, rolled into one figure at the end of the forecast.
terms.why: It is often the largest part of a DCF value, so its assumptions matter most.
terms.how: The terminal growth rate must stay below the discount rate and is usually kept modest; check what share of the total value the terminal value makes up.
terms.formula: Terminal value = Final-year FCF × (1 + g) ÷ (r − g)
terms.finlit: FinLit's DCF calculator works out the terminal value from a terminal growth rate, which must be below the discount rate, or from an exit multiple of year-10 FCF.

terms.meaning: How long a price or NAV stayed below its previous high before getting back to it, or how long it has been below it so far.
terms.why: Two funds with the same worst fall can differ a lot in how long they took to recover.
terms.how: Read it with the drawdown: the drawdown says how deep, time under water says how long.

terms.meaning: The full gain from an investment: price change plus dividends or interest received.
terms.why: Price alone understates returns from dividend-paying stocks.
terms.how: FinLit's total return table adds dividends to price change.
terms.formula: Total return % = (End value − Start value + Income) ÷ Start value × 100

terms.meaning: How far an index fund or ETF's returns drift from the returns of the index it follows, usually stated as a yearly percentage.
terms.why: A small tracking error means the fund follows its index closely; a large one means it often does not.
terms.how: Fees, cash held, and the timing of buying and selling shares all add to it. Compare it between ETFs that follow the same index.
terms.formula: Tracking error = Standard deviation of (fund return − index return)
terms.finlit: FinLit's ETF comparisons work it out from daily price returns against the price index: the standard deviation of the daily differences × √252, shown only with at least 240 overlapping daily returns. Tracking difference, the return gap over the same dates, is shown next to it. Mutual fund pages do not show either yet, because they need index history.
aliases: Tracking error against the price index

terms.meaning: Volume multiplied by price: the rupee value of shares traded in a day.
terms.why: It is the best measure of how easily a stock can be bought or sold.
terms.how: For small investors, a few crore rupees of daily traded value is usually enough; tiny traded values make exits hard.

terms.meaning: An exchange segment where every trade must be settled by delivery, so shares bought cannot be sold the same day. Stocks under surveillance or with other concerns are moved into it, marked on NSE by series such as BE.
terms.why: Such stocks often trade in bursts, and their prices can be less reliable.
terms.how: Check a stock's series before reading its price moves or averages.
terms.finlit: FinLit leaves trade-for-trade (BE) and suspended stocks out of its sector breadth counts.

terms.term: Trading charges (brokerage, STT, stamp duty and others)
terms.meaning: The costs of a trade on top of the price: brokerage, securities transaction tax (STT), exchange transaction charges, the SEBI turnover fee, stamp duty, GST on brokerage and charges, and DP charges when shares leave your demat account.
terms.why: Frequent trading lets charges eat a large part of returns.
terms.how: The contract note for each trade lists every charge; add them up over a year.
terms.finlit: FinLit's portfolio report shows profit and loss after all charges, with a breakdown by type.

terms.meaning: One trading day on the exchange. NSE and BSE equity trading runs from 9:15 am to 3:30 pm IST on weekdays, after a pre-open session from 9:00 am.
terms.why: Many measures count sessions, not calendar days: a 20-session average covers about a month of trading.
terms.how: There are about 250 sessions in a year, 63 in a quarter and 21 in a month.

terms.meaning: How much a fund's NAV changed from a date in the past (one month, six months, one year...) up to the latest NAV.
terms.why: It is the standard way to read a fund's past results over different time spans, all ending today.
terms.how: Trailing returns depend on the day you stop counting, so a fund can look different a month later. Past results do not guarantee future results.
terms.formula:
1-year return = (Latest NAV ÷ NAV one year earlier) − 1
For more than a year: (Latest NAV ÷ Start NAV)^(365 ÷ days between the two NAV dates) − 1
terms.finlit: FinLit takes the start NAV from the latest NAV on or before the start date and states for every figure whether it is a plain change (up to 1 year) or a yearly rate (3 and 5 years).

terms.meaning: A short-term Government of India security (91, 182 or 364 days) issued at a discount and repaid at face value.
terms.why: It is among the safest places for short-term money.
terms.how: Its yield is a common reference for the risk-free rate.

terms.meaning: The general direction of prices over time: up, down or sideways.
terms.why: Trends tend to persist for a while, which is why technical scores watch them.
terms.how: Judge the trend over months, not days.

terms.meaning: A straight line drawn on a price chart through two or more highs or lows to mark the direction of a trend.
terms.why: It makes the slope of a move and its turning points easier to see.
terms.how: Lines drawn by hand are subjective: two people can draw different lines on the same chart. Use them to describe the past.
terms.finlit: FinLit's chart tools let you draw trend lines, horizontal and vertical lines, rectangles and notes on a chart.

terms.meaning: The total of the last four reported quarters, used instead of the last full fiscal year.
terms.why: It gives the most up-to-date yearly figure.
terms.how: P/E and many ratios on FinLit use TTM profit; a ratio marked FY uses the last full year instead.

terms.meaning: A promise, usually by banks, to buy shares that investors do not take up, so the company raises the planned amount. More broadly, judging and taking on a risk, as in loans or insurance.
terms.why: It reduces the risk that an IPO fails.
terms.how: Underwriting is common in SME IPOs, where demand can be thin.

terms.meaning: The share of people in the labour force who are looking for work but do not have it. In India it comes from MoSPI's Periodic Labour Force Survey (PLFS).
terms.why: Jobs drive household income and spending.
terms.how: Compare like with like: the monthly, quarterly and yearly PLFS figures cover different groups.
terms.formula: Unemployment rate = Unemployed ÷ Labour force × 100
terms.finlit: FinLit's macro page shows the monthly rate, published from 2025.

terms.meaning: The paper profit or loss on an investment you still hold.
terms.why: It becomes real (realised) only when you sell.
terms.how: Do not let a paper gain or loss alone decide whether to sell; judge the investment as it is today.
terms.formula: Unrealised gain = Current market value − Purchase cost

terms.meaning: A loan with no collateral, such as a personal loan or credit card, given on the basis of your credit history.
terms.why: Higher risk for the lender means higher interest for you.
terms.how: Repay unsecured debt before investing in shares; its interest usually exceeds expected returns.

terms.meaning: The approval request you accept in your UPI app to block IPO money, used for applications up to ₹5 lakh.
terms.why: Your application is not complete until you approve the mandate.
terms.how: Approve it before the issue closes; mandates expire.

terms.meaning: Working out what an asset or company is worth, and comparing that with its price.
terms.why: Even a great business can be a poor investment if you pay too much for it.
terms.how: Use more than one method: ratios like P/E, comparison with peers and history, and cash-flow based estimates.
terms.formula: DCF value = Sum of FCF in year t ÷ (1 + r)^t

terms.meaning: Style buckets for stocks: value stocks trade at low valuations, growth stocks at high valuations backed by fast growth, and blend sits in between.
terms.why: Styles go in and out of favour; knowing a stock's style explains how it may behave.
terms.how: Mixing styles in a portfolio spreads risk.

terms.meaning: A cost that rises and falls with how much is produced or sold, such as raw materials or delivery charges.
terms.why: Businesses with mostly variable costs are more flexible in downturns.
terms.how: Compare with fixed costs (rent, salaries) to understand how profits react when sales change.
terms.formula: Total cost = Fixed cost + (Variable cost per unit × Units)

terms.meaning: Money invested in young, fast-growing private companies in exchange for a share of ownership.
terms.why: Many such companies fail, but a few successes can return many times the money.
terms.how: Many newly listed Indian companies were funded by venture capital; their IPOs often include VC sellers (see Offer for sale).

terms.meaning: How much a price swings up and down, usually measured as the standard deviation of returns and stated per year.
terms.why: Higher volatility means a bumpier ride and more chance of large short-term losses.
terms.how: A stock with 21% yearly volatility often moves around 1.3% on a typical day.
terms.formula: Volatility = Standard deviation of returns
terms.finlit: FinLit's yearly volatility uses the last 60 daily returns scaled by √252.

terms.meaning: A stretch when a share's daily price range narrows well below its usual width. A breakout from a squeeze is the first strong move out of the narrow range.
terms.why: Quiet spells are often followed by bigger moves, though not in a predictable direction.
terms.how: A squeeze says a larger move may come, not which way it will go.
terms.finlit: In FinLit's short-term technical view a breakout from a squeeze counts +1, a squeeze with positive momentum +0.5, any other squeeze −0.25 and unusually wide volatility −0.5.

terms.meaning: The number of shares traded in a period, usually a day.
terms.why: Price moves on high volume carry more weight than moves on thin volume.
terms.how: FinLit's 'volume spike' alert fires when volume is several times its 20-day average.

terms.term: Volume profile (value area and point of control)
terms.meaning: A count of how much volume traded at each price over a period. The point of control is the price with the most volume; the value area is the band around it where most of the volume, usually about 70%, traded.
terms.why: It shows the prices where most trading happened, and where there was little.
terms.how: Compare the value area of the latest swing with the one before: a higher value area means trading has moved up to higher prices.
terms.finlit: FinLit's short-term technical view compares this swing's value area with the previous swing's: entirely higher +1, centre higher +0.5, centre lower −0.5, entirely lower −1.

terms.meaning: The blended yearly cost of a company's funding: the return shareholders expect plus the after-tax interest on its debt, weighted by how much of each it uses.
terms.why: A company creates value only when its return on capital beats its WACC.
terms.how: Compare ROCE with WACC: ROCE above WACC is good news.
terms.formula: WACC = (E ÷ V) × Re + (D ÷ V) × Rd × (1 − Tax rate)

terms.meaning: Your list of stocks to follow, with notes and price targets.
terms.why: It keeps research organised and lets FinLit show you what changed.
terms.how: Add a one-line reason for each stock so you remember why you are watching it.

terms.meaning: The average number of shares outstanding during a period, with each share counted for the part of the period it existed.
terms.why: EPS divides profit by this figure, not by the count on the last day, so a mid-year share issue counts only for the months it was outstanding.
terms.how: If shares were issued late in the year, this number sits below the year-end count.
terms.formula: Weighted average shares = Σ (shares outstanding × fraction of the period outstanding)

terms.meaning: The share of closed trades that ended in a profit.
terms.why: It shows how often trades worked, but not how much was made or lost on each.
terms.how: Read it with the average gain and the average loss: a 40% win rate can still make money if the gains are much bigger than the losses.
terms.formula: Win rate % = Winning trades ÷ All closed trades × 100

terms.meaning: The money tied up in day-to-day operations: short-term assets (cash, inventory, receivables) minus short-term liabilities (payables, short-term debt).
terms.why: Too little can mean trouble paying bills; too much means cash is stuck in stock and unpaid invoices.
terms.how: Compare working capital with sales over several years; a sharp rise needs an explanation.
terms.formula: Working capital = Current assets − Current liabilities

terms.meaning: eXtensible Business Reporting Language: a standard format for tagging financial statements so computers can read them.
terms.why: Indian companies file results with the exchanges in XBRL, which is how platforms like FinLit collect data.
terms.how: When a figure looks odd, compare it with the company's PDF filing; tagging errors do happen.

terms.meaning: The annualised return for investments made on different dates, such as monthly SIPs.
terms.why: Simple returns mislead when money goes in at many different times; XIRR handles that.
terms.how: Use XIRR to judge your SIP or portfolio returns. Spreadsheet programs have an XIRR function.
terms.formula: 0 = Sum of CF_i ÷ (1 + XIRR)^((d_i − d_0) ÷ 365)

terms.meaning: The change in a figure compared with the same period a year earlier, such as Jun 2026 quarter against Jun 2025 quarter.
terms.why: It removes seasonal effects, like festive-season sales.
terms.how: Use YoY for quarterly results; use QoQ to spot turning points.
terms.formula: YoY % = (This period − Same period last year) ÷ Same period last year × 100
aliases: Operating profit growth, year on year
Profit growth vs same quarter last year
Sales growth vs same quarter last year

terms.meaning: The income an investment pays each year as a percentage of its price.
terms.why: It lets you compare income from shares, bonds and deposits.
terms.how: A yield that looks too good to be true usually reflects high risk.
terms.formula: Current yield = Yearly income ÷ Current price

terms.meaning: The total yearly return you would earn on a bond if you hold it until maturity and every payment is made.
terms.why: It is the fairest way to compare bonds with different prices and coupons.
terms.how: When interest rates rise, bond prices fall and YTMs rise.
terms.formula: Price = Sum of C ÷ (1 + YTM)^t + Face value ÷ (1 + YTM)^n

terms.meaning: Building each budget from zero, justifying every expense, instead of starting from last year's figures.
terms.why: It cuts costs that only continue out of habit.
terms.how: Companies that adopt it sometimes show sharp margin gains; check that they last.

terms.meaning: A bond that pays no regular interest. It is sold below face value and repays face value at maturity; the difference is your return.
terms.why: Its price swings more with interest rates than ordinary bonds.
terms.how: Useful for a known future expense if held to maturity.
terms.formula: Price = Face value ÷ (1 + r)^n
